World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: 'It's pretty touching': Students pen postcards to thank veterans
World.content:
This Anzac Day, Van Reuben is one of thousands of children across Queensland sending postcards to former and serving Australian Defence Force members.

Using red crayons, the year 5 student adds poppies to his postcard as he talks about his dad's time in the army during the war in Afghanistan.

Van Reuben is among thousands of Queensland students who have written a postcard to a veteran. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"It makes me feel glad that he fought for all the people and for our country," Van said.

"Anzac Day is special to me because I get to commemorate all those people who fought for me and I get to commemorate my dad."

Darra State School is among 190 schools across Queensland taking part in the Returned and Services League's (RSL) Postcards of Honour program.

Loading

Connecting generations

The initiative encouraging students to connect through writing a postcard to a local veteran has been running for four years.

As part of the program, a veteran from a local sub-branch attends a school to deliver a presentation about the importance of the day and the history behind the Anzacs.

Grant Hartigan says the postcards are a "tangible token of gratitude" for veterans. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Darra RSL president Grant Hartigan toured Iraq after joining the army in 2014 as an infantryman and spoke at Darra State School this year.

What it takes to make an Anzac Day wreath A remembrance tradition that Australians have adapted to commemorate fallen soldiers has ancient Greek and Roman origins.

"Seeing some of the veterans' faces when they receive these postcards is just indescribable," he said.

"Especially when they realise kids from the local school were thankful for older Australians and veteran service. It's pretty touching.

"It really gets engagement from the younger generation where they get an opportunity to show remembrance and also give a tangible token of gratitude to servicemen and women."

The exchanging of postcards is also symbolic, mimicking the events of World War I, when frontline soldiers would send postcards home to their loved ones.

Tracy Freeman says listening to veterans like Grant Hartigan helps students learn and understand. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

It's an activity Darra State High School Principal Tracy Freeman feels have helped students connect to veterans through creativity and empathy.

"Listening to Grant really helps our children to connect with their feelings and empathise how the soldiers may have felt back in the Anzac period," she said.

"The students are able to learn, they're able to connect and they're able to show gratitude to the servicemen before us and it's just across generations."

World.title: Bus replacements mean some V/Line commuters can't get to work on time
World.content:
A couple of years back, David Oborne moved to Birregurra which is about a two-hour drive west of Melbourne.

He grew up in the region and figured he would still be able catch the train to work in Melbourne a few times a week.

On weekdays, a 6:20am bus from Birregurra gets commuters to Waurn Ponds station in time for the 7:21am V/Line train to Melbourne which arrives at Southern Cross at 8:36am.

"When it works it's great, but when it's not, it's not," Mr Oborne said.

Earlier this month — amid skyrocketing petrol prices — trains were replaced with buses for line maintenance.

The earliest replacement service does not get to the city until 10:40am.

Commuters on the Warrnambool line are now forced to either drive an hour or more to the nearest station with an earlier service — typically Wyndham Vale — or all the way to Melbourne.

"It's pretty disappointing that we haven't got that like-for-like service," Mr Oborne said.

"Fuel prices are ridiculous at the moment and for me, to fill up to drive to Melbourne and back three times a week, there's no real benefit in it … it's costing you 300-odd dollars a week."

" It's not as if we can opt out of going to work. "

V/Line trains leaving Southern Cross station have been packed during the free travel period. (ABC News: James Oaten)

Then there's the issue of getting home.

"The other day it was a nightmare," he said.

"Leaving work, you get on a 5:10 train back to Wyndham Vale and then there are not enough buses to be able to accommodate the people on that train which resulted in me getting home at quarter-to-nine at night, opposed to getting on the train and coming to Birregurra at nearly seven o'clock.

"Not being able to get home on time does make it bloody hard."

Passengers wait to board the V/Line replacement bus service at Waurn Ponds station in Geelong. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Commuters on the Warrnambool and Geelong lines have been impacted by replacement bus services from April 11 to 24 to allow for maintenance and upgrade works along the line.

It was announced last week that the Warrnambool and Colac lines replacement services would continue until May 20.

The replacement services have coincided with increased passenger numbers due to Victoria's free public transport, with many V/Line commuters complaining about overcrowding on regional services.

But lack of like-for-like replacement services — running earlier buses so passengers can reach their destination at the same time as a rail service — has become a particular cause of irritation for those on the Warrnambool line.

Some V/Line passengers taking up the free public transport offer are finding their services replaced by buses that take longer to get to their destination. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Public Transport Users Association regional spokesperson Paul Westcott said scheduled line maintenance was an "unavoidable necessity" but the lack of early replacement services was unacceptable.

"You would think it was incumbent on the V/Line to offer a like-for-like [replacement service] if a train service is cancelled for maintenance or is discontinued for a while," Mr Westcott said.

"It's just not acceptable to cancel a train or to stop running a train for maintenance and then not provide a like service with the replacement buses.

"Obviously, there are fewer public transport services in the regions so the ones that are there are very valuable, and people have to build their schedules around those relatively infrequent services."

Liberal MP Richard Riordan says regional commuters should receive the same standard of service as city users. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Polwarth state Liberal MP Richard Riordan said the lack of earlier replacement services was "simply not fair".

"Public transport and good connections from our regions into the city are vital," Mr Riordan said.

"You can't be arriving in Melbourne at lunchtime, particularly if you're elderly or disabled, and then expect to get your specialist medical appointments.

" People in Melbourne … would not cop public transport — free public transport — that didn't get you into the city until lunchtime. "

Mr Riordan called on V/Line to provide a like-for-like service for commuters affected by the Warrnambool and Colac line upgrade.

V/Line says the bus replacements allow for important rail upgrades that will improve safety and reliability for commuters. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

When asked if the replacement coach service timetable for the Warrnambool line would be updated to include earlier services, V/Line said it would review customer feedback and explore if adjustments were necessary.

"We're delivering important maintenance upgrades to the Warrnambool and Geelong lines throughout April and May to ensure the continued safety and reliability for passengers," a V/Line spokesperson said.

"We thank passengers for their patience and ask them to allow extra time to get to their destination while replacement coaches are operating."

The state government announced over the weekend that it would extend the free public transport period until the end of May.

Yesterday, it announced the 2026/27 budget would include funding for more V/Line services on the Shepparton line as well as the Belgrave, Lilydale, Glen Waverley, Alamein, Mernda and Hurstbridge lines in Melbourne.

But the full roll out may not be operational until next year.

World.title: Buyers eyeing troubled smelter, administrators say, as workers face job decision
World.content:
The administrator of the Liberty Bell Bay manganese smelter in northern Tasmania is confident the underlying business is viable and a buyer will be found among the Australian and international bidders who have expressed interest.

"It's definitely a viable business," Morgan Kelly, of Ernst and Young, told the ABC.

"It's a business that's got great potential in terms of its earning capability."

" I am confident that we will achieve a sale. It's all subject to confidentiality [but] we have a mix of Australian-domiciled and international interested parties. "

The smelter is a major employer for George Town. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Kelly said the bids received under the non-binding indicative offer process, which closed on Friday, were "absolutely" predicated on keeping the 216-strong workforce intact.

"There's a very strong desire to retain the full workforce," he said.

Liberty Bell Bay production manager Health Williams says government support is needed. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

"A major part of what we're selling here is we've got a really great supplier network, we've got a really great customer network, we've got an operating smelter, and we've got a fantastic workforce which is ready to return to work.

"So that's a very important part of the sale process, and a very big part of the value of [what] we're selling."

Liberty Bell Bay was placed into voluntary administration last month by private equity firm White Oak, which had been a secured lender to parent entity Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance, which collapsed last year.

Liberty Bell Bay enters voluntary administration The owner of Australia's only manganese alloy smelter has entered voluntary administration. It means further uncertainty for the Tasmanian smelter's workforce.

Mr Kelly said Liberty Bell Bay had been cash-starved under the ownership of GFG.

"It's really a question of capital constraint rather than anything else, which has caused challenges for this business, and that's impacting us in the administration process as well."

On Thursday, the administrators EY told workers there was no more money to continue paying wages beyond this week and about 175 would be faced with the choice of taking leave without pay or facing redundancy.

Those have been given until the end of today to make a decision.

Workers have been given until today to decide if they will take leave without pay, or lose their job. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Kelly declined to say what proportion of the workforce would choose to go unpaid, but said the main objective of administrators was to keep the workforce "intact".

"We're [making] some adjustments to the workforce to allow us more time to be able to continue very limited operations while we move through phase two due diligence, but we're confident that those workforce changes will be temporary," Mr Kelly said.

"Our main objective is to keep the workforce intact.

"We're just trying to make it as short a period of time as humanly possible that anyone's without pay, but at the same time trying to keep everybody or keep the workforce available because it's a workforce with a highly specialised skill set, which is critical to this asset," he said.

Hundreds of Liberty Bell Bay workers and their families turned out to Monday's event. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Mr Kelly said he could not put a definite timeframe on the next phase of the sale process, which is conducting due diligence on the bidders, but said site inspections were being scheduled this week and he was "hoping to be well advanced within the next three to four weeks."

Smelter workers plead for government support as final payday looms Tasmanian smelter workers at risk of losing their salaries are pleading with the state and federal governments to step in — pointing to large bailouts given to other companies.

Hundreds of workers and their families attended a rally in George Town on Monday, at which union leaders and politicians spoke in support of the workforce and called for state and federal governments to intervene.

Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone chief executive Susie Bower said administrators had indicated two to six weeks of bridging funds were needed until a new buyer could be brought in.

" I think that is kind of optimistic from a due diligence point of view, but if the administrators can make it work, then let's make it work. "

Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone CEO Susie Bower says administrators had indicated two to six weeks of bridging funds were needed. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The AWU estimates the weekly wages bill at Liberty Bell Bay is $1.6 million and Chris Donovan, assistant national secretary, said only $5 million was needed to cover workers until a sale is finalised.

"When you look at the hundreds of millions of dollars, and in some cases billions of dollars, that other state and federal government have put into smelters that have run into trouble, this five million dollars is a measly amount," Mr Donovan said.

Chris Donovan, assistant national secretary of the Australian Workers' Union, spoke at Monday's rally. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Nothing 'concrete' from governments

Mr Kelly said the administrators had "very positive" discussions with both the state and federal government and had "strong indications of support".

However, he said, "we haven't had any offers [or] any discussions around anything concrete."

Tasmanian infrastructure minister Kerry Vincent said yesterday a proposal for a support package had been put to the federal government and he expected quick progress, but couldn't say when a resolution will come.

"There is a package being put forward to the federal government to assist the workers and community and we'll continue to have talks to the federal government," Mr Vincent said.

Liberty Bell Bay smelter workers are facing an uncertain future. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Federal Bass MP Jess Teesdale told the rally she was pleased to hear the Tasmanian Government had put a support package proposal to the Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres.

Smelter workers told to take leave without pay or be sacked About 175 workers at Australia's only manganese smelter, Liberty Bell Bay, have been told they will be laid off at the end of next week unless they take leave without pay.

"There are a lot of potential buyers in the wings here, and we just need to make sure that the actual value of that facility, which is its people, are there for that sale," she said.

A spokesperson for federal industry minister Tim Ayres said the workforce was facing "unacceptable uncertainty" after being let down by GFG.

"The administrators, who are funded by White Oak, are pursuing a rapid sales process for the assets," they said.

"The Liberty Bell Bay workforce is a core part of the value of that sale and must be recognised and treated as such throughout the process.

"The Australian government has worked and is continuing to work closely with the Tasmanian Government to ensure workers and local suppliers are supported and receive appropriate assistance."

Heath Williams had support from his kids at the rally. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Workers nervous, but hopeful

Generations of George Town families have worked at the smelter and local businesses and schools would suffer if it never reopened.

Liberty Bell Bay production manager Health Williams said the smelter was a profitable business with "the right owner".

"I'm hoping that the government will lend a lot of support to get it in the right hands because that's what it needs," he said.

Attending this morning, Mr Williams said he was nervous, but hopeful of a positive outcome.

EY's Mr Kelly told the ABC that, including all off-balance sheet liabilities, the liability to employee creditors was about $34 million and there was in excess of $20 million owed to unsecured creditors.

"We've only had the first meeting of creditors and we haven't called for proofs of debt or adjudicated on those yet, and I haven't even talked about the inter-company loans, which are very complicated," he said.

World.title: Giant's debut and a taunted Aussie in spotlight as NBA playoffs begin
World.content:
The first round of the NBA playoffs are officially underway with a series of Game 1s taking place across the league.

If you're ever wanting to dream up an epic playoffs, you'd likely ask for a mix of heroic returns from injuries, stars performing at the absolute peak of their powers and a little bit of bad blood thrown in there. This year's first round has all these elements.

A host of young stars and teams are making their playoff debuts, while seasoned veterans are hoping to cement legacies. Everyone is hunting Oklahoma City, last year's NBA champion.

Here is what to watch out for in of the first round series.

Eastern Conference

(1) Detroit Pistons vs (8) Orlando Magic

SEASON SERIES: Tied 2-2

Cade Cunningham has recovered from a collapsed lung in time for Detroit's playoff run. (Getty Images: David Jensen)

Cade Cunningham is back just in time for Detroit's post-season after missing 11 games with a collapsed left lung.

Detroit thrived in Cunningham's absence, going 8-3 while he sat as his teammates elevated their games.

Jalen Duren has elevated his points, rebounds and assists numbers post-All-Star break, while Daniss Jenkins stepped into Cunningham's starting spot with aplomb.

Detroit has been a surprise packet this season, but there will be no surprises in the playoffs where teams have extensive scouting time in the lead-up to, and during, a series.

As opponents look to take Cunningham out as much as possible, the elevation of those around him will be key to the Pistons making a deep run.

Games involving the Pistons are almost always messy — this is a team that is literally and figuratively a pack of street-fighters, both in their style of play and their demeanour.

The Pistons are matched up against an opponent in Orlando, that is as comfortable as just about any team in the NBA when it comes to mucking it up.

Expect this series to look like something out of the mid-2000s, and if you're looking to place money on a brawl, this series is the place to do so as well.

(2) Boston Celtics vs (7) Philadelphia 76ers

SEASON SERIES: Tied 2-2

Jayson Tatum's stunning return from an Achilles rupture has Boston dreaming of winning another NBA title this season. (Getty Images: Winslow Townson)

After more than successfully holding the fort ahead of Jayson Tatum's return from an Achilles rupture, Boston heads into the playoffs as the favourite to advance to the NBA Finals out of the Eastern Conference.

Tatum's shooting numbers are still not back to his peak levels, but the rest of his game has returned to his pre-injury levels.

Boston has been excellent offensively all season long, but its offence in clutch situations will be what to look out for this year.

The Celtics struggled mightily in this department last year, often reverting to isolation ball when things got tight, with Tatum particularly guilty of this.

Paul George (left) and Tyrese Maxey (right) must carry the Sixers in the absence of Joel Embiid to begin the playoffs. (Getty Images: Emilee Chinn)

Boston had the worst offence in clutch situations in last year's playoffs, and is still without a prototypical floor general.

Jaylen Brown has elevated himself as a playmaker this year, averaging a career-high 5.2 assists per game, and the Celtics will rely on him to set the table for his teammates more effectively than he was able to do 12 months ago.

Boston's first-round opponent Philadelphia will look for All-Star guard Tyrese Maxey to replicate his regular season form which saw him light up the Celtics to the tune of 30 points per game across four meetings this season.

Can Philly hang tough in this series and extend it out long enough to give Joel Embiid a chance to return from a recent appendectomy?

(3) New York Knicks vs (6) Atlanta Hawks

SEASON SERIES: New York won 2-1

Jalen Brunson will have to contend with Atlanta's bevy of wing defenders, including Australia's Dyson Daniels. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

The best version of the Knicks is good enough to make the Finals. Just how often that version appears in the playoffs is anyone's guess.

New York has played Jekyll and Hyde all season long en-route to the third seed in the East this year.

Despite the inconsistencies, this is a team that ended the regular season ranking inside the top 10 in both offence and defence.

The Knicks will be frustrated that they've got to face one of the league's hottest teams in Atlanta in what shapes as a gruelling first-round series.

Atlanta went 20-6 after the All-Star break, the league's third-best record behind Oklahoma City and San Antonio, and did so using a stout defence which ranked second behind the Thunder after the break.

Australia's Dyson Daniels will draw the primary assignment on Knicks star Jalen Brunson, and the pair already have a history of run-ins, making for a spicy match-up.

While Daniels didn't match his astronomical steals tallies from a season ago, he still remains one of the NBA's best perimeter stoppers, and his wiry strength and quickness will no doubt annoy Brunson.

Bookmakers have this series as one of the hottest picks to be a first-round upset, given how closely matched these two teams are.

(4) Cleveland Cavaliers vs (5) Toronto Raptors

SEASON SERIES: Toronto won 3-0

The Cavaliers enter the playoffs as one of the teams under most pressure to perform after a series of disappointing early exits. (Getty Images: Jason Miller)

There is perhaps no team in the NBA that is under more pressure to have a deep run heading into the playoffs than Cleveland.

The Cavs' last two post-season trips have been undone by a combination of poor health and a lack of composure in big moments, and the Cavs have once again fought the injury bug all season long en-route to a 52-30 record.

Cleveland is finally whole as the playoffs get underway, but it remains to be seen whether their best players have had enough minutes on the court together.

Not a single five-man line-up for the Cavs has logged over 100 minutes this season. The line-up with the most minutes played, 89, contains two players who aren't on the roster anymore. In comparison, Toronto's starting five has logged 354 minutes together.

The match-up between Evan Mobley (left) and Scottie Barnes (right) will be a major swingpoint in the series. (Getty Images: Jason Miller)

The Cavs and Raptors are virtually exact opposites of each other in the sense that Cleveland has an elite offence and middling defence, while Toronto has a middling offence and an elite defence.

While they may not directly guard each other at all times, the match-up between Cleveland's Evan Mobley and Toronto's Scottie Barnes, the No.3 and No.4 picks in the 2021 draft respectively, is tantalising.

The Raptors ranked 21st in the league in three-point percentage during the regular season, and the Cavs will dare them to make shots from the outside to win this series.

Cleveland's opponents shot the third-best percentage from long range during the regular season, and if this trend continues, the Cavs could be heading home early.

Western Conference

(1) Oklahoma City Thunder vs (8) Phoenix Suns

SEASON SERIES: Oklahoma City won 3-2

Oklahoma City is finally whole as they look to become the NBA's first repeat champions since 2018. (Getty Images: Joshua Gateley)

The Thunder have backed up last season's championship with as dominant a season as you'd like to see out of a defending champion.

OKC enters the playoffs as the hot favourite to go back-to-back, but recent history has shown that the playoffs don't always pan out as expected for return champs, with no team having defended its title since Golden State in 2018.

Having battled injuries all season long, the Thunder finally have a full rotation to call on for the start of the post-season and will use this series to tune up for the rest of the playoffs.

The Thunder finished the regular season with the seventh-best offence and the best defence and the miserly defence will once again be its calling card.

OKC faces a surprise-packet Phoenix team, who ousted Golden State in the play-in game to pick up the eighth seed.

Everything about this series suggests the Suns are overmatched, but what they lack in talent, they make up for with a boatload of heart.

Phoenix ranked 17th in the league in offence this season, and that lack of scoring firepower means you're dead on arrival against the Thunder.

The Suns' best offensive players are all perimeter operators. The only problem with that is the Thunder are blessed with perhaps the league's best suite of perimeter defenders. That is a nightmare match-up.

(2) San Antonio Spurs vs (7) Portland Trail Blazers

SEASON SERIES: San Antonio won 2-1

Victor Wembanyama (left) makes his long-awaited playoff debut after a dominant season on both ends of the floor. (Getty Images: Ronald Cortes)

San Antonio's rise from a non-playoff team last season to legit contender this season is one of the stories of the season.

Luckily for this Spurs core, they will make their playoff debut against a team in Portland, whose core also has no playoff reps.

The Spurs went 24-4 after the All-Star break, including a 22-2 record in games where Victor Wembanyama played, and also posted the NBA's best net rating in that period.

Wembanyama is already the league's most impactful defender and in possessions where he is on the floor, San Antonio's opponents score at a rate only marginally better than the worst offensive team in the NBA, Brooklyn.

Portland is also a feel-good story this season, and thrust itself into the seventh seed courtesy of a superhuman play-in performance from Deni Avdija.

Avdija was at the heart of everything good offensively for the Blazers this season, and ranked third in the NBA on free throws per game.

Avdija has averaged 31.7 points and eight assists in three outings against the Spurs this season, and also shot over 52 per cent on threes, well above his season average of 31.8 per cent from long range.

The Blazers will also turn to defensive stoppers Toumani Camara and Jrue Holiday to handle the Spurs star guard trio of Stephon Castle, De'Aaron Fox and Dylan Harper.

(3) Denver Nuggets vs (6) Minnesota Timberwolves

SEASON SERIES: Denver won 3-1

Nikola Jokic (left) comes into the playoffs on the back of one of the most dominant regular seasons of all-time. (Getty Images: Aaron Ontiveroz)

In what feels like one of the better Western Conference rivalries, the Nuggets and Wolves face-off in a series for the third time in four years, with the current ledger reading 1-1.

Minnesota finished the regular season with a whimper, going 8-7 in its last 15 games, with most of those coming in the absence of the injured Anthony Edwards.

Edwards is back for the Nuggets series, but just how healthy he is remains to be seen. If he's not near 100 per cent, the Wolves are virtually dead on arrival.

Denver went through its own malaise during the regular season, with that coinciding with injuries to Nikola Jokic, Aaron Gordon and Payton Watson, but have gotten healthy at the right time.

The health status of Anthony Edwards (runner's knee) will be a major watch throughout this series. (Getty Images: Aaron Ontiveroz)

The Nuggets went 13-2 in their last 15 games, and crucially got some minutes into the Jokic-Gordon-Jamal Murray line-up that blew the doors off opponents.

Jokic has put together one of the greatest seasons in league history, becoming the first player in NBA history to lead the league in both rebounds and assists per game.

Minnesota's four-time Defensive Player of the Year Rudy Gobert will once again be tasked with the Jokic assignment, and it'll really be all about damage control.

Julius Randle was a pleasant surprise for the Wolves during last year's playoffs and will need to be just as efficient in this series if Minnesota is to advance.

(4) Houston Rockets vs Los Angeles Lakers

SEASON SERIES: Los Angeles won 2-1

Kevin Durant (left) and LeBron James (right) have previously only met in NBA Finals in 2012, 2017 and 2018. (Getty Images: Alex Stilz)

What a treat it is to get another Kevin Durant-LeBron James series in the playoffs for the first time since the 2018 NBA Finals.

The Lakers come into the series decimated by injuries with both Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves sidelined, meaning it is up to James, 41, to carry the load for the umpteenth time in his 23-season career.

James had looked as spritely as a 41-year-old can look prior to the Dončić and Reaves injuries as he settled into being the third option for the Lakers, and will have to summon something from his prime years to keep Los Angeles alive for long enough for at least Dončić to return after visiting Spain to treat his hamstring.

Houston owns the eighth-best offence for the entire season, but has slipped to 13th after the All-Star break, and the Lakers will hope that slippage allows them to hang around, even while understrength.

Luka Dončić's potential return date hovers as a swing factor for this series. (AP Photo: Lynne Sladky)

James has shot just 30.9 per cent from three-point range this season, his lowest mark since the 2015-16 season, and he'll need his three to have a revival to be able to go blow-for-blow with Durant and the Rockets.

Houston, while amassing over 50 wins during the regular season, has been one of the league's poorest teams in late-game situations.

The NBA defines 'clutch' minutes as situations in the last five minutes of the fourth quarter or overtime where the margin is either five points or less, and the Rockets come into the playoffs as the seventh-worst team in such situations.

Offence gets tougher in the playoffs and how efficient Houston is able to be on that end will determine just how far it can go in the post-season.

World.title: Snapshot of Australia's relationship with cash over the past two decades
World.content:
Before the global financial crisis, the ubiquity of internet banking and the advent of contactless payments — cash was king.

More than two-thirds of transactions made in Australia were by cash in 2007.

In 2025, it was about 15 per cent.

But according to The Reserve Bank of Australia's 2025 Consumer Payments Survey, for the first time in decades, cash use has increased, albeit slightly.

Cash use reached its lowest ebb in 2022, falling by more than 50 per cent from the previous reporting period in 2019.

Coinciding with the small rise in cash payments was an increase in the amount of in-person transactions, which lifted from 16 per cent in 2022 to 19 per cent in 2025.

Payments under $10 continued to be the most popular size of cash transaction.

But the volume of these transactions is still just a sliver of what it was 20 years ago, when 95 per cent of payments under $10 were made with cash.

What are Australians spending their cash on?

The survey found that cash use either stabilised or increased across every consumer spending category.

Leisure has moved to top spot on cash spending ahead of food, retail and transport, which has seen the largest fall of any other spending category since 2007.

The report authors highlight this is likely due to the use of contactless payments, growth in ride-share services, and the use of digital payments in most public transport systems.

"Australians have consistently used cash more frequently to pay for leisure," the survey reads.

The Commonwealth announced prior to the last election it would require businesses to accept cash as payment for groceries, fuel and other essentials.

Prior to the policy, which came into effect at the beginning of the year, about 94 per cent of businesses in the country accepted cash payments.

At present, Australia has one cash distributor, Armaguard, after it acquired rival Prosegur in 2023.

Last year the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) allowed the Australian Banking Association's members to collaborate ways to ensure cash could continue to flow around the country in the event Armaguard was no longer able to do the job, giving them until December 2026 to come up with a solution.

How frequently are Australians using cash?

The report found around half of Australians use cash on a weekly basis.

The report identified 1.5 million Australians as 'high cash users', meaning they pay with cash for 80 per cent of their transactions.

They made up about 7 per cent of respondents, which was about the same as the previous reporting period in 2022.

"The share of respondents who did not use cash at all in the survey week was relatively stable between 2022 and 2025, at around 50 per cent," the survey read.

But when survey authors asked respondents about their cash use outside of the survey period, only 13 per cent said they never used cash.

The survey found people who used cash as a larger portion of their transactions tended to be older, and in lower-income households.

It found about 10 per cent of respondents over 65 used cash for all their transactions in 2025.

Report authors highlighted cash was integral for vulnerable communities who had less payment options.

They also said cash was important for those who struggled to gain access online banking such as those living in remote areas including First Nations communities.

The downward trend of cash use was starting to reverse across demographics.

"The share of payments made with cash was stable not only among high cash users, but also among respondents of different ages, incomes and locations over the three years to 2025," the report read.

"This contrasts with the results from previous surveys, which showed a trend decline in the use of cash across all demographic groups."

How do Australians feel about cash?

About a third of survey respondents said they would face hardship or a major inconvenience if they were not able to withdraw cash.

Around 20 per cent said they used cash to avoid paying surcharges.

In March, the RBA announced it would remove surcharges on debit and credit cards, which will come into effect on October 1.

The report found about two in five respondents carry cash in their wallets for emergencies.

It also found three quarters of those surveyed held cash in their wallets in 2025 with the median held around $65.

"Suggesting that they could cover a typical in-person payment during a short outage affecting electronic payments by using the cash in their wallets," the report read.

World.title: He was deported to Tonga. What he did there was calculated to 'p*** off' Australia
World.content:
An Australian deportee serving a life sentence in Tonga for importing methamphetamine has confessed he attempted to set up a chapter of the Comancheros in the island nation to "piss off" the Australian government.

Eneasi Taumoefolau's 2024 arrest on drugs charges made international headlines, igniting fears the notoriously violent outlaw motorcycle gang had infiltrated the nation known as "the Friendly Islands".

Speaking exclusively to Foreign Correspondent inside a Tongan prison, Taumoefolau claimed he never fully succeeded in establishing the "Kingdom Chapter" as his effort was thwarted by the unsophisticated level of criminality in Tonga.

"It was just stupid," he said. "I was reckless and I was very ambitious in the way I thought 'I'll do it because it'll really, really piss them off.'"

Taumoefolau was deported to Tonga from Australia in 2022, having been previously convicted of drug trafficking offences and jailed.

Late last year, the 44-year-old was convicted of importing more than 2 kilograms of methamphetamine into Tonga from the US and sentenced to life in prison.

Eneasi Taumoefolau was sentenced to life in a Tongan jail. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

A Comancheros tattoo on Taumoefolau's leg. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

He agreed to an interview, conducted inside Hu'atolitoli Prison, in part because he believes he's been unfairly portrayed as a "poster boy" for deportees facing a harsh stance on drug crime.

Tongans who have been deported from Australia, New Zealand and the US, after receiving criminal convictions or overstaying visas, are overrepresented in Tonga's prison population.

The sentence for importing class A drugs like methamphetamine in Tonga is life for amounts of 28 grams or more, and Tongan authorities told the ABC the country's jails were overcrowded with drug crime offenders.

While the sentences can be tough, the freedoms afforded to inmates are surprising.

Hu'atolitoli Prison has no fence and escapes are not unheard of. When Foreign Correspondent arrived, Taumoefolau was smoking a cigarette on a bench outside his cell.

Tonga's Hu'atolitoli Prison grounds. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

Inmates in Tonga's Hu'atolitoli Prison. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

His leg sports a large tattoo of the Comancheros club logo, which he said he got after he was deported back to Tonga.

"Maybe it's a bit obvious, but yeah, I don't regret getting it. I just shouldn't have put it so in people's faces," he said.

#comancheroboss

Taumoefolau and his family left Tonga when he was around eight years old.

As an adult he became involved in Sydney's criminal underworld and eventually a prospect for the Hell's Angels bikie gang.

"All of my own faults, that's how that happened. I grew up in a very normal family," he said. "I guess it's led to where I am today, my own decisions."

In sentencing remarks from a drug conviction 15 years ago, a judge observed that Taumoefolau's criminality "involved succumbing to the temptation of easy money".

After he was deported back to Tonga, he lived lavishly, holing up in Nuku'alofa's most expensive hotel and posting his exploits on TikTok.

"I think I was still bitter at the Australian government for deporting me," he said.

"It was just from the day I knew I was coming back to the days I spent in detention, that's all we ever got told, that you're not going to succeed anywhere or go back and do anything."

Taumoefolau's TikTok videos. (Supplied)

His TikTok videos featured bags of cash, luxury cars and heavily referenced gangs and outlaw motorcycle groups.

Taumoefolau promoted himself as the #comancheroboss, living the #comancherolife, and even donned a T-shirt with a Comanchero patch as he filmed himself getting a haircut.

"The TikTok thing, I understand it, and it was just me having a dig it there. It wasn't nothing else, and that's the honest truth," he said.

When police later discovered Comancheros vests, patches and a motorbike bearing the group's insignia, it became evidence of his plan to form a "Kingdom Chapter" of the outlaw motorcycle gang.

"I got the patches thinking I was going to do that," he said. "But then when I seen the way the culture was, it was dismantled because I had to be the one that answered for everything.

"The sophisticated, whatever it is, that had to be done — it's not here. The criminal underworld that I find, even in the prison, is not here. It's not intelligent to the level we would consider doing that. So, it got dismantled."

The Comancheros have strict rules — it's been said that the only way to leave the club is in a body bag — and Taumoefolau says he couldn't be sure prospective members in Tonga would follow the gang's code.

Comancheros vests and patches were used as evidence of Taumoefolau's plans to start a "Kingdom Chapter" of the outlaw gang in Tonga. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

Patches reading "Comancheros Tonga" in police evidence. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

"For example, like snitching or talking or stuff like that, it's so normal here for them to just talk," he said.

Even among his fellow inmates, including some serving years for small quantities of drugs, "they just told on themselves", he said.

"This island here and the culture here and the kids here, they're not — I'm just talking about sophisticated, organised crime — they're not on the level."

Police in Australia describe the Comancheros as a violent organised crime group, involved in large-scale drug importation, firearms trafficking, extortion and gangland style executions.

Taumoefolau's younger brother, Christian, was the sergeant-at-arms for the Victorian branch and is currently serving a life sentence for the murder of Mitat Rasimi, which a judge described as "brutal, barbaric and callous".

Police in Tonga were certainly concerned about the level of criminal sophistication that an established presence of the Comancheros in the country would bring.

"The biggest danger really is around connecting with already long-established connections that exist for drug supply from South-East Asia and South America," said Tonga Police Commissioner Geoff Turner.

Tonga Police Commissioner Geoff Turner. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

Appointed to the top job last year, the former Commander of Specialist Operations for the Australian Federal Police believes Tonga has a growing gang influence, rather than a gang culture.

"I think we had an opportunity there and did a very good job on shutting down an outlaw motorcycle gang, the Comancheros, in Tonga," he said.

Turner is now overseeing an intelligence review to establish what level of gang membership and influence still exists in Tonga.

"It's a very small market, people are known to each other. We've got very good street intelligence, which you would expect from [a] population this small."

Operation Burrito

Street intelligence is what led to Taumoefolau's arrest, as part of a highly secretive, targeted police effort dubbed "Operation Burrito".

Its origins go back to February 2024, when a police sergeant who had observed the drastic increase of methamphetamine in Tonga managed to recruit an informant he knew through church.

The informant brought police into a local plot to import several kilos of methamphetamine into Tonga from the United States, which resulted in 17 arrests.

Drone footage obtained by the ABC shows how police eventually made their dramatic arrest while Taumoefolau was leaving his house in Tofoa.

Taumoefolau is seen placing a red bag, containing packages of methamphetamine, into a car and driving away, moments before a police car blocks his path and officers drag him out of the car.

Another man, drove off in a separate direction only to be ambushed by an unmarked car containing armed members of Tonga's Tactical Response Group, who shot into his engine as he was trying to reverse.

Loading...

A police raid on a storage unit and a vehicle also discovered a startling array of Comancheros gear inscribed with "Kingdom of Tonga", "President" and "Sergeant-at-arms".

Deputy Commissioner Tevita Vailea, who oversaw the operation, believes it showed an organised gang structure with intent; he believes there were already close to ten members and plans to recruit many more.

"To be honest, we did not expect that much. But it's clearly the evidence of how much they wanted to set up and establish it," he said.

Vailea showed the items confiscated to the ABC, among them Taumoefolau's motorbike, now held in a secure location by Tonga Police, which brandishes the slogan "ACCA" — Always Comanchero, Comanchero Always.

Taumoefolau is now awaiting a verdict in his trial for participating in an organised criminal group, which concluded hearing evidence in Tonga's Supreme Court last week and is expected to return its decision at a later date.

The same court had earlier heard that the methamphetamine importation, like much of the drugs that come into Tonga, arrived in a shipping consignment from the US.

Tonga Police Deputy Commissioner Tevita Vailea. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

More Tongans live outside the country than within and there is a large Tongan diaspora in the US.

According to court documents, as the financier of the drug importation Taumoefolau paid $74,739 TOP ($43,000) to a man in California, said to be for the transfer of two or three Harley Davidson motorcycles.

"Out of every good job, another two or three jobs kick off. So without going into too much detail, there are other investigations ongoing and we are working with US authorities," said Tonga Police Commissioner, Geoff Turner.

"Our short to medium term goal is to certainly make that progress to do that extradition or have charges laid in the US."

Taumoefolau said he was planning to appeal his conviction for methamphetamine importation, which would now require special leave to be granted, as the initial window to lodge an appeal has closed.

Life in a tiny cell

When Taumoefolau walked Foreign Correspondent through the prison cell where he may spend the rest of his life, he described his new reality as "eye-opening".

Taking the key to his own cell out of his pocket, he let himself back into the cell after our interview.

"I wasn't expecting company," he said with a chuckle, apologising for the mess.

His cell is tiny, without electricity or lights — although inmates are allowed candles — and it is extremely hot.

It's impossible not to notice how small it is for a man like Taumoefolau, a former professional fighter with a bulking frame, let alone for both him and his cellmate.

There's "nothing more important than religion" in the jail, Taumoefolau says. (Foreign Correspondent: Stephanie March)

"I grew up in Australia, so I've never thought that this is the cell I'm gonna end up in, for the rest of my life, essentially," he said.

In an unexpected way, he said his incarceration has allowed him to connect with Tongan culture for the first time in his life.

"Here, nothing's more important than religion. So I'm getting more and more of the religion than anything," he said.

"They made me pray the other day — it was weird. It was fulfilling, but I've never done anything like that, but they don't give you a choice here. You have to do it."

While prayer may be a new concept to him, there's already a sense of penitence creeping into his reflections on life.

"This is not a good life. For those who think that they're going to go join a gang and be involved with this brotherly organisation, the walk is very lonely and you do it by yourself," he said.

"I think a lot of those young men are confused about what's really coming and how that life really turns out."

Watch Part 2 of Foreign Correspondent's special investigation into drugs in the Pacific, tonight at 7.55pm on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: NRL overhauls training rules in landmark player safety move
World.content:
In a major safety move, the National Rugby League has capped contact in training in a bid to reduce injuries including concussion.

The ABC can reveal all 17 NRL and 12 NRLW clubs have been informed of the development, with guidelines limiting the minutes of contact in both in-season and pre-season training sessions.

The move to restrict training loads is aimed at mitigating injuries, including brain injuries, which continue to be a major issue for all contact sports.

All 17 NRL clubs were informed on the eve of the season that their players are to engage in no more than 100 minutes on a regular seven-day turnaround.

In the NRLW, whose 2026 season begins in July, female players can engage in no more than 85 minutes per week on a seven-day turnaround.

All of this training is inclusive of wrestling.

For the NRL and NRLW it is no more than 40 or 50 minutes of contact on a five- or six-day turnaround.

The new preseason guidelines place limits of no more than 200 minutes for men and 115 minutes of contact per week for women.

Sports neuroscientists and neurologists had previously called for Australia's major leagues, the NRL and AFL, to restrict contact in training to protect footballers from concussions and subconcussive impacts.

World Rugby and the US's National Football League have already implemented contact restrictions for their athletes in both their preseason and in-season training sessions, to lessen the number of impacts to the brain.

Until now, there have been no set limits on contact training in the NRL and NRLW, with the head coach of the club determining the intensity and physicality of training.

NRL sources say in the last two decades contact in training has exponentially increased.

Do you know more? Contact Jessica Halloran at Halloran.Jessica@abc.net.au

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page.

Preseason has traditionally been the most physical and high-contact segment of the year for NRL and NRLW players but now the coaching hierarchy have been given a set of guidelines.

These new guidelines are for the first time formally encouraging moderation.

In the preseason later this year the men will be instructed to have a limit of "contact training to no more than 100 minutes per week pre-Christmas (inclusive of wrestling training)".

The NRL also state clubs should:

Limit total contact training to no more than 200 minutes per week post-Christmas (inclusive of wrestling training).

Avoid high intensity contact training on consecutive days.

Schedule no more than three consecutive days of contact training without a recovery day.

The 12 NRLW clubs have been told that during their pre-season this June they should:

Limit total contact training to no more than 115 minutes per week, with no more than 35 minutes of high-intensity contact.

Avoid high intensity contact training on consecutive days.

Schedule no more than three consecutive days of contact training without a recovery day.

There is also a "graded introduction protocol" for both men and women where from day one to five of their respective preseasons there is no physical contact.

On day one of pre-season training both NRL and NRLW clubs must "restrict activities to physical screenings, meetings, classroom education and general conditioning. No football-specific training equipment, or team-based drills".

On days two to five of preseason the guidelines say clubs should limit training to "non-contact, skill-based drills only. No live or high-intensity contact".

Clubs were told the proposed guidelines for the NRLW were based on a survey of NRLW clubs and analysis compiled on the men's data.

But the guidelines could evolve.

Clubs have been told "the contact rules are intended to be iterative while the research is ongoing and data from the 2026 season will be used to inform contact training rules for the 2027 season".

Inside a brain with suspected CTE The effect of head knocks over Gordi Kirkbank-Ellis's decades-long sporting career isn't immediately obvious. That is, until you see what's happening to his brain.

Clubs will be required to log contact — but questions remain about how the rules will be policed. Several sources say that policing the compliance to the training restrictions will be key to the policy's success.

The move by the NRL follows similar measures by other sporting bodies which like them have faced and are facing legal action from players who say they have sustained brain injuries during their careers.

The NFL first implemented a reduction in contact in 2011 and has since paid out $1 billion in compensation for football-related brain injuries.

World Rugby placed restrictions on contact in training in 2021.

World Rugby guidelines for professional teams include restricting full-contact training to a maximum of 15 minutes per week and controlled contact (using pads and shields) to 40 minutes per week. They also include a 30-minute weekly cap on live set-piece training.

Players like former Roosters captain Luke Keary have previously called on the NRL to cap the contact in training.

"We should have had less contact five years ago," Keary said in 2023.

"They do it in the NFL. I don't know how we haven't done those studies and tests … I just don't know how it hasn't happened."

In 2024 the NRL introduced efforts to monitor concussion away from games and updated protocols during training.

Each club is currently now required to film every contact training session they conduct, with footage used to analyse any potential concussion risks during training.

The degenerative brain disease Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy, which is linked to repetitive hits, has been found post-mortem in the brains of rugby league players including Rothman's medal winner Paul Green and Canterbury Bulldogs star Steve Folkes.

Keith Titmuss — a Manly Sea Eagles player who also played schoolboy rugby union for Newington College in Sydney — was also found to have CTE at just 20.

The AFL still has not formally reduced contact in training.

Shane Tuck playing for Richmond in 2012. (AAP: Joe Castro, file photo)

After Richmond player Shane Tuck died by suicide at 38 — and was found to have CTE — there was a coronial inquiry into his death.

In 2023, coroner John Cain Jr made a number of safety recommendations including that the league implements restrictions to contact in training.

Last month the Herald Sun reported the AFL had been tracking contact training data across six intensity categories from warm-up drills at the low end to full match simulations and could limit training minutes as early as 2027.

AFL football executive Laura Kane told the Herald Sun: "But we are happy to confirm there is no correlation between how much contact training you do and the ladder [positions] and there hasn't been for the two full seasons since the coroner's recommendation [to cut contact training]."

If you or anyone you know needs help: Lifeline on 13 11 14

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

The AFL is currently facing a class action of 100 footballers who claim they have been left brain injured by the game.

More than 500 AFL players will soon no longer be covered by insurance for brain injuries in their superannuation, after Zurich Insurance moved to cut their ability to claim for concussion and head trauma from May 1 this year.

Zurich Insurance recently told the ABC there was "widespread uncertainty" around the potential magnitude of CTE and the long-term effects of concussion.

One NRL club source, who wished to stay anonymous, said they expected rugby league's move to be embraced positively by most teams.

"The sentiment is that as long as it is done sensibly and with consultation, I don't think the opposition to these guidelines will be high," they said.

World.title: Answering the big questions you might have about the NDIS
World.content:
Life changing supports, cost blow outs, cuts, and rorts — the discussion around the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) is wide ranging.

It's a massive, complex scheme, and it can be difficult to know the difference between fact and fiction.

On Wednesday, federal minister Mark Butler will address the National Press Club with a significant announcement about the scheme's future.

Ahead of that, we answer some of the biggest questions around the scheme.

Why did the NDIS start?

In a sentence: To replace a broken, state‑based system with a national guarantee of support for people with significant disability.

In a few more: The NDIS had a staged roll out that began in 2013 after years of campaigning by people with disability, their families and advocates.

The scheme was announced by the Gillard government and passed parliament with bipartisan support.

"The consequences of disability — isolation, poverty, loss of dignity, stress, hopelessness and fear of the future — can be avoided … the National Disability Insurance Scheme is the greatest change to Australian social policy in a generation," Gillard told the House of Representatives in 2012.

Prior to the scheme, disability services were fragmented across states and territories.

People with the most profound conditions struggled to access basic support to go to the toilet and use vital equipment such as wheelchairs. Others lived in large institutions and families struggled to care for their children.

What are the NDIS's benefits?

In a sentence: The scheme has dramatically improved life for those it supports and it's not just welfare — it helps participants give back to the economy.

In a few more: The NDIS has been transformative for participants, providing basic assistance to many for the very first time.

It has helped some shower and eat in their own homes, and allowed others to move from large institutions where violence and abuse thrived and into smaller specialised accommodation with essential supports.

Many participants have also been able to develop skills to be independent, find work and contribute to society. Think tank Per Capita estimated in 2021 that for every dollar spent on the NDIS, $2.25 was returned to the economy.

Huge numbers of jobs and businesses have also been created to support those participants.

Where is the NDIS at now?

In a sentence: It now supports about 760,000 people and costs more than $50 billion a year, making it one of the largest items in the federal budget.

In a few more: The NDIS became fully operational in 2020, when the annual cost was hovering around $20 billion, and seven years after its staged rollout began.

Now, spending on the scheme has reached $50 billion a year. It's more expensive than Medicare and is closing in on defence spending.

The NDIS is now growing at 10.3 per cent per year, making it the second fastest growing form of federal expenditure, behind paying back the national debt.

Various changes to the scheme in recent years have halved its growth rate from 22 per cent per annum. That's where it was when the Albanese government was elected in 2022.

The government wants to get it down to at least 5-6 per cent per year.

How did the costs blow out?

In a sentence: An influx of participants, especially autistic children; a lack of regulation; and states and territories shutting down their services.

In a few more: When the NDIS was set up, the Productivity Commission projected a mature scheme would support about 400,000 participants, costing about $13.5 billion a year.

Now, the NDIS supports 760,000 participants — about 1 in 40 Australians directly, according to the government — and is set to cost more than $50 billion this financial year.

The scheme's architects assumed there would be stricter eligibility, tighter guardrails, and that the children receiving early intervention would improve and leave the scheme.

But once the NDIS began, previous state-run services closed, leading the scheme to become what ministers like to call the "only lifeboat in the ocean".

It meant that a scheme initially designed to support only those with significant and permanent disabilities absorbed more and more people, especially kids and those with autism.

Inconsistencies in the current planning process have seen some people be dramatically overserviced compared to someone else with the same disability or level of impairment.

Fraud and non-compliance have also become a huge problem.

How widespread is fraud?

In a sentence: We don't know exactly, but it's a result of a lack of guardrails at the outset of the scheme.

In a few more: The extent of fraud is difficult to nail down, but it's become a big issue — and a key driver of the scheme's recent reputational hit.

NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister last month requested another inquiry into the extent of fraud and non-compliance (things like billing breaches and poor documentation) in the scheme, suggesting even she doesn't know the true scale.

In 2024, the acting boss for the NDIS watchdog, the Quality and Safeguards Commission (QSC), said more than a fifth of all funding could be being abused by criminals.

The QSC itself wasn't established until 2018 — five years after the scheme first started its rollout.

That, coupled with a poor payment tracking system, and not enough checks and balances on who delivers services and their quality, are thought to be why fraud has taken such a hold.

A statement released in March said the government's fraud task force established in 2022 has 660 active investigations, and seen 59 people referred to court, leading to 23 convictions.

While fraud isn't the top driver of overall cost growth, it remains a key target for the government.

Where does the money go?

In a sentence: Support workers, carers, therapies, assistive technology, accessibility modifications and more.

In a few more: Supports are broken up into three categories:

Core supports help participants with everyday activities. These are things like a support worker to assist with a doctor's visit, a carer to provide personal assistance at home, a cleaner coming into a participant's home, or consumables such as continence products or foot braces.

help participants with everyday activities. These are things like a support worker to assist with a doctor's visit, a carer to provide personal assistance at home, a cleaner coming into a participant's home, or consumables such as continence products or foot braces. Capacity building supports help build independence. This stream is what pays for things like therapies and training to help bolster employment opportunities.

help build independence. This stream is what pays for things like therapies and training to help bolster employment opportunities. Capital supports are bigger ticket items — think higher-cost pieces of assistive technology, equipment and home or vehicle modifications.

Core supports accounted for almost 80 per cent of all funding last calendar year. One of the reasons why is because core supports includes payments to participants in Supported Independent Living (SIL).

SIL is support that assists participants to live independently in their home. It often involves round-the-clock supervision and is particularly expensive due to the complex needs of the residents.

The average package per participant in 2025 was just under $66,700, while the median package was $19,300.

It's skewed this way due to a very small number of participants receiving very high cost supports and a large number receiving low cost supports.

Participants can only use their funding on services pre-approved in their plan, and changes introduced in 2024 further tightened what the scheme could cover.

How much can providers charge?

In a sentence: It changes, depending on the service, where a participant lives, travel and the time of day.

In a few more: The maximum a provider can charge for a service is set out yearly in a complex price guide, though amounts can also vary depending on a participant's location, the time of day and how much travel is involved, and the evidence base of a therapy.

In the 2025-26 price guide, assistance with self-care activities during the day on a weekday is capped at $70.23 per hour. If that participant is in a very remote location, the cap is $105.35 per hour. If it's a public holiday, it's $156.03 and $234.05 per hour respectively.

The standard cap for house cleaning that a participant can't do themselves is $58.03 an hour, while rates for a physio and other therapies are $193.99 an hour.

Providers can also bill for travel time. Therapists can bill 50 per cent of their hourly rate for travel. So, if a physiotherapist travelled for an hour to deliver support, they could claim a maximum of $97.00 (50 per cent of their hourly cap of $193.99).

A criticism of this flat model has been that experience or qualification are not always taken into account. For example, a support worker with limited training could come in for low-level support and charge the same amount as a skilled nurse coming in to administer a feeding tube.

Providers have been critical of how the caps have evolved, saying while the price of delivering service has increased, how much they can charge hasn't risen at the same rate.

Does the NDIS pay for sex and haircuts?

In a word: No.

In a few more: Lists introduced in late 2024 made it very clear what services were ruled out for participants to spend their funds on, including sex work and therapies with limited evidence bases such as scuba, cuddle and equine therapies.

Participants can apply for something not on one of these lists to be covered by the scheme if they can prove it provides better outcomes and value for money than something that is on the lists.

Things like haircuts are not covered by the scheme.

While you might've seen headlines about the NDIS paying for this, what's generally being funded is a support worker taking the participant there safely, and not the haircut itself.

How many providers are there?

In a sentence: Nearly 280,000 — but only 6 per cent are registered and visible to regulators.

In a few more: There were 276,581 active NDIS providers in the December 2025 quarter.

However, 94 per cent, or almost 260,000, weren't registered with the scheme watchdog.

Currently, registration for many providers is voluntary. It's not illegal to be unregistered, though these providers don't need to go through audits or notify authorities of deaths.

Essentially, the scheme watchdog has very little oversight of unregistered providers, knows little about them, and has limited powers to reprimand them.

In July, the government is introducing mandatory registration for SIL accommodation and online platforms matching participants with support workers to give authorities greater visibility over who operates in the market. It's expected similar registration requirements will soon be expanded to other providers.

Pinning down exactly how many providers are in one area isn't as easy as it might look.

While the NDIS' provider finder tool can help narrow down how many providers operate in a particular suburb, it's imperfect. It only lists registered providers, and also includes online services that can be accessed from anywhere in the country, meaning not everything that shows up is physically located there.

Views on registration vary greatly across the disability community, while providers have complained about the red tape and costs involved under the current system.

Who is and isn't on the NDIS?

In a sentence: The biggest cohorts are autistic people and kids — and the vast majority of Australians with disability aren't on the scheme.

In a few more: Autism is, by far, the most common primary condition for participants.

Children with autism or developmental delay make up almost half of all people on the NDIS.

Last year, it was revealed about 16 per cent of all six-year-old boys in Australia were on the NDIS.

While that number is undeniably high, many of those kids won't be on the scheme for life. That's because the early intervention pathway for kids — which aims to lessen the lifelong impact of their disability by providing support at the earliest possible stage — ends at age nine.

Overall, rates of NDIS participation rise steeply from birth, peaking at approximately 12 per cent at age six. It falls to around 1 per cent at ages 35-40, before slightly rising to 2.5 per cent by age 65.

While the scheme now supports 760,000 participants, that's only 14 per cent of the 5.5 million Australians estimated by the Bureau of Statistics to be living with disability.

People over 65 cannot apply for the NDIS, but can remain on it after that age if they were a participant before. The government maintains over-65s are better looked after by the aged care system.

What's happening next?

In a sentence: More cost-cutting changes, including a new, lower-touch program for some kids under nine to direct them off the NDIS.

In a few more: The ballooning cost of the scheme has forced the federal government to introduce a raft of changes set to come in this year.

A new program called Thriving Kids will divert children under the age of nine with "mild to moderate" developmental delay and autism off the scheme over time, starting in October.

In July, it will be mandatory for providers of SIL or online platforms that connect participants with supports to be registered with the NDIS.

There will also be a shake up to the way plans are formulated with a controversial new assessment tool rolling out — the finer details of which still haven't been released.

On top of that, July will see the start of a new set of price caps.

More changes are expected to be announced this week.

World.title: FBI director sues over article portraying him as MIA, problem drinker
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS politics FBI director sues over article portraying him as MIA, problem drinker Michael Koziol April 21, 2026 — 5:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Washington: FBI director Kash Patel is suing The Atlantic magazine over an explosive article that portrayed him as “missing in action” and a problem drinker whose behaviour has alarmed those around him at the nation’s top crime-fighting agency. The article, published on Friday, said multiple witnesses described Patel’s “bouts of excessive drinking”, and reported that there was widespread concern in the US government about his conspicuous intoxication. FBI director Kash Patel is suing The Atlantic magazine over an article portraying him as unreliable and a problem drinker. Bloomberg Multiple times in the past year, members of Patel’s security detail “had difficulty waking [him] because he was seemingly intoxicated”, The Atlantic reported, citing “information supplied to Justice Department and White House officials”. The magazine alleged that at one point, staff made a request for “breaching equipment” – ramming gear used by SWAT and hostage teams to enter buildings – because Patel was unreachable behind a locked door.



Patel’s colleagues are reportedly concerned his behaviour has become a threat to public safety, and that he may be missing or unavailable while the nation responds to a domestic terrorist attack. A Donald Trump loyalist and a national security official during the first Trump administration, Patel was appointed by the president in part to reform the FBI after what both men believe was the politicisation and weaponisation of the agency under Trump’s predecessor Joe Biden. Donald Trump has not made a public declaration of support for Kash Patel since The Atlantic published its story. Bloomberg In the lawsuit, filed in the US District Court for the District of Columbia on Monday morning (US time), Patel’s lawyers said The Atlantic article constituted a “sweeping, malicious, and defamatory hit piece” that crossed a legal line and contained “false and obviously fabricated allegations”. The journalist, Sarah Fitzpatrick, “could not get a single person to go on the record in defence of these outrageous allegations”, the complaint said, and instead relied on anonymous sources “she knew to be both highly partisan with an axe to grind and also not in a position to know the facts”.



Patel also accused the magazine of a “well-documented, long-running editorial animus” against him, failing to give him enough time to respond to their questions and “deliberately structuring the pre-publication process to avoid receiving information that would refute their narrative”. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Sucking up to Trump will always be a losing battle. Just ask Pam and Kristi Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist The Atlantic said in a statement that it stood by its reporting and would vigorously defend itself and Fitzpatrick against the “meritless lawsuit”. Rumours have circled in Washington about Patel’s fate as FBI director, with anonymous sources briefing media outlets that Trump was dissatisfied with him, among other senior appointees and cabinet members. While on official travel to Italy for this year’s Winter Olympics, Patel was filmed chugging beer in the locker room with the American men’s hockey team after they won a gold medal, in a clip that went viral.



Patel gave an interview to Fox News on Sunday (US time) in which he blamed the “fake news mafia” for trying to destroy his reputation and foreshadowed that he would sue for defamation. He also defended his record on reducing violent crime, cutting opiate overdose deaths, seizing fentanyl and reducing the flow of the killer drug into the US. Homicides plunged more than 20 per cent in 2025, and are on track to be the lowest since 1900 when data is finalised, according to the Council on Criminal Justice. “If I’m not doing my job, if I’m not working, then how is it that the FBI delivered the safest America under President Trump’s leadership in the history of our country?” Patel said on Fox News. Trump has not made a public declaration of support for Patel since The Atlantic published its story. But White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told the magazine that crime had plummeted under Patel’s leadership of the FBI and he “remains a critical player on the administration’s law and order team”.



If Trump were to move against Patel, the FBI director would join a growing list of top appointees purged in recent months, after Kristi Noem was ousted as homeland security secretary and Pam Bondi removed as the attorney-general. The FBI is of particular concern to Trump. Its investigation of alleged collusion between Russia and senior officials in the Trump 2016 campaign dominated the early stages of his first term, and led him to fire James Comey as FBI director in 2017. Trump continues to regard Comey as one of his political enemies, and in his second term, he pressured Bondi and the Justice Department to bring charges against Comey. Those charges – that he lied to Congress – were thrown out after a judge found they were improperly brought.
